questions.question: Butter rises from R60 to R85 a brick after a dairy shortage. Describe, in words, what happens in the MARGARINE market, naming the kind of related good and the kind of change on the demand diagram.
questions.expected_answer: Butter and margarine are substitutes — they answer the same want. Margarine's own price has not changed, so this is not a movement along margarine's demand curve. The entire margarine demand curve shifts to the right: at every possible margarine price, more margarine is demanded, and the market settles at a new equilibrium with a higher margarine price and larger quantity. Rule: a rise in the price of a substitute shifts demand for the other good to the right.

questions.question: Define derived demand, and trace BOTH directions of the loop between product markets and factor markets using the Western Cape rooftop-solar boom.
questions.expected_answer: Derived demand is demand in a factor market that is borrowed from demand in a product market — electricians are demanded because powered homes are demanded. Forward: the solar boom raises product demand, so firms demand more electricians, panels, inverters and finance — installer wages and factor prices get bid up. Backward: those higher wages and component prices are production costs, shifting supply in the product market leftward and lifting installation prices. The circular flow adds a third link: factor incomes return as household spending in product markets.

questions.question: Name the four market structures, rank them by number of sellers and ease of entry, give a South African example of each, and state which are imperfect markets and why.
questions.expected_answer: Perfect competition (very many sellers, identical products, free entry — one cabbage farmer among hundreds at a fresh-produce market); monopolistic competition (many sellers, differentiated products, easy entry — coffee shops, takeaways, hair salons); oligopoly (few large sellers, hard entry, interdependence — supermarket groups, mobile networks, domestic airlines); monopoly (one seller, no close substitute, blocked entry — the freight-rail network or the water pipes to a street). Perfect competition is the only perfect market; the other three are imperfect because their sellers hold some power over price.
